arXiv:2607.23191v1 [cs.LG] 25 Jul 2026

Wrong Design Intent Is Worse Than None: A Derangement-Control Diagnosis of Header Conditioning in CAD Program Completion

Yang Xiao Affiliation: Sichuan University Email: yangx64519@gmail.com
Abstract

Fine-tuned code LLMs can be conditioned on a lightweight design-intent header to steer parametric CAD generation, but whether the model actually reads the header’s content has not been tested under a metric independent of the conditioning itself, nor with a causal control. We study CADCON, a five-feature design-intent header prepended to CadQuery-style sketch-extrude programs during LoRA fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B, re-scored by executable geometric assertions on the produced B-rep solid, sharing no code with the header-defining regex extractor. Across three seeds and a pre-registered {0%, 40%}-prefix ×\times {correct, wrong, masked}-header matrix we find: (i) in conditional completion (40% prefix), a semantically wrong header degrades adherence below the no-header baseline (0.43 →\rightarrow 0.30/0.21 text/token) on design intents the model can render unconditioned — polygonal and thin geometries; circle and tall intents sit at a baseline generation floor for this checkpoint (≈\approx0 in both compared arms) and are uninformative for this contrast; (ii) a derangement control — retrained with shuffled ground-truth headers, identical header marginal but destroyed content correlation — remains competent yet is immune to wrong headers, while the standard model is not (text headers; interaction significant on 3/3 seeds, p ≤\leq 4.2×10−34.2\times 10^{-3}): the harm requires the learned header→\rightarrowprogram mapping, excluding the marginal/mechanical distribution-shift confound; (iii) the independent metric deflates the apparent benefit of a correct header (token: +0.21 regex →\rightarrow +0.02 geometry), quantifying metric circularity; (iv) the harm is regime-specific — at 0% prefix the unconditioned baseline cannot generate valid CAD at all. Wrong intent is not noise: it actively misdirects generation.

1 Introduction

Parametric CAD encodes not just geometry but design intent — the shape classes, proportions, and topology a part is meant to have. As code-pretrained LLMs are fine-tuned to emit sketch-extrude programs, a practical question follows: can we steer that intent with a lightweight specification, and does the model actually read the specification, or merely respond to the presence of a trained field? The distinction is a deployment hazard: a model that has learned to depend on a conditioning field can fail silently — or worse — when that field is absent or wrong.

Prior work conditions CAD generation on natural language, images, or point clouds and reports that conditioning “works” Xie and Ju (2025); Guan et al. (2025); Wu et al. (2021). But three questions have gone unexamined in structured geometric generation. First, what happens when the conditioning content is wrong: does the model ignore it (graceful), or trust it and generate something worse than it would have unconditioned (hazardous)? Second, if wrong content hurts, is that because the model reads the content — or merely because any mismatched header is an out-of-distribution input? Third, is the reported benefit of conditioning real, or partly an artifact of scoring adherence with the same feature detector used to build the conditioning target?

We answer all three with CADCON (CAD CONditioning), a five-feature design-intent header (CIRCLE, NGON, THIN, TALL, MULTI_PART) prepended to CadQuery-style sketch-extrude programs — transpiled from DeepCAD histories — during LoRA fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B. Two methodological moves carry the paper (Figure 1). Metric independence: adherence is re-scored by executable assertions on the produced B-rep solid (in the style of CADTests Mallis et al. (2026)), sharing no code with the training-side regex extractor; the evaluation matrix — {0%, 40%} program prefix ×\times {correct, wrong, masked} header, three seeds, both tokenizations — and all decision rules were frozen before scoring. Causal control: we retrain the model with deranged ground-truth headers — every training program receives another program’s header, so the header marginal is byte-identical but the header↔\leftrightarrowprogram correlation is destroyed — and test whether this control, which cannot have learned a header→\rightarrowprogram mapping, is also hurt by wrong headers at evaluation. Throughout, “causally controlled” refers specifically to this design: it isolates the learned header→\rightarrowprogram mapping as the cause of the harm, excluding the marginal/mechanical distribution-shift confound; the finer mechanism — graded semantic reading versus learned consistency-checking — is explicitly out of scope (§5).

Our findings:

  1. 1.

    A semantically wrong header hurts more than no header. In the conditional-completion regime (40% prefix), a wrong header degrades geometric adherence below the no-header baseline (0.425 →\rightarrow 0.305 text / 0.215 token), direction-unanimous across three seeds and both tokenizations (token side p ≤\leq 8×10−48\times 10^{-4} on every seed, two seeds ≈\approx10−510^{-5}), surviving on the valid-geometry subset — so it is not a validity artifact. The effect holds on design intents the model can render unconditioned (polygonal / thin); circle and tall intents sit at a generation floor for this checkpoint (≈\approx0 adherence in both the baseline and wrong-header arms) and are uninformative for this contrast.

  2. 2.

    The harm requires the learned header→\rightarrowprogram mapping. A derangement-trained control remains competent yet shows no correct→\rightarrowwrong drop, while the standard model drops sharply (text headers; interaction positive and significant on 3/3 seeds, p = 4.2×10−34.2\times 10^{-3} / 6.7×10−66.7\times 10^{-6} / 3.6×10−63.6\times 10^{-6}); the control realizes an identical geometric feature set under correct and wrong headers on 71–98% of jointly-executable outputs (93%/71%/98% per seed), versus 35–43% for the standard model. The marginal/mechanical distribution-shift confound is thereby excluded (§4.4). To our knowledge this is the first isolation of wrong-content-worse-than-no-content, with a causal control, in structured geometric program generation.

  3. 3.

    The independent metric deflates the conditioning benefit. The apparent gain of a correct header shrinks relative to the regex metric (text +31% vs +52% relative; token +4% vs +46%), quantifying a real, previously only-bounded metric circularity in conditioning claims — while the wrong-header harm is preserved on both metrics.

  4. 4.

    The harm is regime-specific. At 0% prefix the unconditioned baseline cannot produce valid CAD at all (0/100 executable, floored at zero adherence); “wrong < none” is undefined there and does not hold. The effect lives specifically in conditional completion, where a meaningful baseline exists.

Together, these findings argue for rewriting the default risk model of intent conditioning in structured generation — a model in which, as §2 documents, work on conditioned structured generation tests whether the signal is present or how good it is, but never what happens when it is wrong. On the benefit side, in our setting conditioning delivers less than its own self-referential evaluation reports (finding 3): most of the token-header gain is metric circularity, which argues that conditioning claims in this literature should routinely be read against conditioning-independent, execution-level evaluation. On the harm side, a natural worst-case assumption for a conditioning interface — that a bad signal at most degrades the model toward its unconditioned behavior — fails in our setting (finding 1) — a failure that extends to structured geometric generation what misleading-context work documents in natural language Tao and Agrawal (2026); and the dissociation (finding 2) locates the cause: the damage requires the learned header→\rightarrowprogram mapping and is not a mechanical reaction to a rare or malformed input (§4.4). That localization matters for repair as much as for diagnosis — it implies that mitigation belongs at the conditioning interface itself, not in input validation: a well-formed wrong header passes any format check. And because the harm is confined to conditional completion (finding 4) — editing and extending existing designs, precisely the workflow such models are being built for — the hazard sits in the intended primary use case, not in a corner case.

The contribution is diagnostic, not a new architecture, but the diagnosis carries a design principle, a portable method, and an agenda. The design principle: a trained conditioning field is a trust interface — once a model has learned to rely on it, upstream errors (a stale user specification, a retrieved description, or, as in plan-conditioned pipelines (§2.2), another model’s inferred plan) are not filtered out but routed into generation, so graceful degradation toward unconditioned behavior — rather than letting the error steer generation — must be designed in, not retrofitted. The method: the audit pair used here — an execution-level metric sharing no code with the extractor that defines the conditioning signal, plus a derangement-trained control that separates harm requiring the learned mapping from a mechanical reaction to an off-distribution input — is not specific to CAD: wherever the conditioning signal can be shuffled at training time and adherence can be scored independently of that signal, the pair offers a template for interrogating a “the model follows X” claim in conditioned generation. The agenda: the diagnosis makes sharp follow-up questions visible — whether the deflation and the harm persist at scale and across representations; which content-dependent reading holds (graded semantic reading or learned consistency-checking) — the grain our dose-response probe could not resolve (§5); and how to detect or absorb wrong intent at decode time. CADCON is the vehicle: a metric-independent, causally controlled testbed for characterizing when intent conditioning helps, when it is over-credited, and when it actively harms.

2 Related Work

2.1 Generative models for parametric CAD sequences

Neural parametric CAD modeling began with dedicated architectures over construction sequences. DeepCAD Wu et al. (2021) introduced the first generative model for CAD operation sequences, together with the large-scale dataset of sketch-extrude histories from which our corpus derives. SkexGen Xu et al. (2022) encodes topological, geometric, and extrusion variation into disentangled codebooks, giving users coarse control over which properties the generated sequences share. SolidGen Jayaraman et al. (2022) bypasses construction sequences altogether, autoregressively predicting vertices, edges, and faces to synthesize boundary representations directly. A second wave fine-tunes pretrained code LLMs. CADmium Govindarajan et al. (2025) pairs more than 170k CAD models with human-like textual descriptions and fine-tunes a code LLM for text-driven sequential design. FlexCAD Zhang et al. (2024) renders a CAD model as structured text and fine-tunes an LLM into a single controllable generator across all construction hierarchies, from sketch-extrusion down to individual curves. CAD-Recode Rukhovich et al. (2024) represents sketch-extrude sequences as executable Python code and translates point clouds into CadQuery programs — the program representation also used here. Across both waves, these systems model the distribution of valid CAD models and are evaluated on generation or reconstruction quality — including, for the controllable ones, whether a requested property can be produced. Whether the model is faithful to the semantic content of a conditioning signal, and what happens when that content is wrong, sits outside their evaluation scope; that question is ours.

2.2 Conditioning quality vs. conditioning presence

Prior intent- and text-conditioned CAD generation varies the quality — or at most the presence — of a conditioning signal, but never its correctness. ToolCAD Gong et al. (2026) evaluates text-to-CAD across the abstract-to-expert prompt levels (L0–L3) inherited from Text2CAD, with every condition receiving some correct prompt and no unconditioned control. ProCAD / “Clarify Before You Draw” Yuan et al. (2026) detects under-specified or internally conflicting CAD prompts and repairs them via clarification, rather than measuring the cost of following a wrong one. Closest to our setting, CAD-HLLM Zuo et al. (2025) fine-tunes a parameter-completion model conditioned on an inferred symbolic plan — a trained conditioning field, like our header — and ablates the plan away (showing generation degrades without it), yet never evaluates a plan that is wrong: the correctness axis of a conditioning signal that the model has learned to depend on remains untested. In the natural-language setting, misleading context is known to depress conditioned generation below the no-context baseline: Tao & Agrawal (2026, Findings of ACL) Tao and Agrawal (2026) formalize a “do-no-harm” requirement for context-conditioned generation — naming neutral regression the case where a model overwrites a correct answer under an effectively non-informative context — and empirically document that plausible-but-misleading distractor contexts push standard with-context decoding well below the no-context baseline (e.g., 60.4 →\rightarrow 36.2 for Llama-3.1-8B), which their two-stream decoder mitigates by backing off to the no-context stream. In retrieval-augmented QA, MADAM-RAG Wang et al. (2025) mitigates misinformation in retrieved evidence and notes that a closed-book baseline can sometimes beat naive RAG; MisBench Peng et al. (2025) measures preference for in-context misinformation under knowledge conflict in multiple-choice QA. These establish that a wrong conditioning signal can be worse than none in natural language; none isolates this in conditional structured geometric generation — nor, to our knowledge, does any pair it with a trained control that separates harm requiring the learned mapping from a mechanical reaction to input mismatch, as our derangement control does (§3.7).

(We deliberately do not adopt the term ‘‘neutral regression’’ for our effect: it is defined for non-informative context, whereas our wrong header carries incorrect content --- the analog is the distractor case above.)11 1 We do not cite AlphaCode’s metadata ablation as a wrong-vs-none precedent: on inspection it establishes no such ordering — its incorrect-solution tag hurts only relative to the correct tag, and at the largest sample budget the no-tag condition is in fact lowest.

2.3 Code models under corrupted or misleading signals (contrast)

Waheed et al. Waheed et al. (2025) apply controlled perturbations to code fine-tuning data and find reasoning is far more vulnerable to structural than to semantic corruption — “even corrupted code with misleading signals remains competitive when surface-level regularities persist.” CodeCrash Lam et al. (2025) moves the manipulation to inference time, injecting misleading natural-language contexts — false comments, plausible-but-incorrect hints, and misleading print statements — into input code and finding substantial degradation of LLM code-reasoning accuracy. Both contrast with our setting: Waheed et al. perturb training data (ours is an inference-time conditioning field), and CodeCrash measures program understanding in off-the-shelf models — its misleading-vs-vanilla contrast quantifies distraction through a channel the model was never trained to rely on, not the correctness axis of a conditioning field the model has learned to depend on (ours is conditional structured generation through exactly such a field). That semantic corruption is often tolerable in code reasoning sharpens the interest of a setting — ours — where a semantically wrong signal is actively harmful.

3 Method

Figure 1 overviews the method: the header-construction pipeline and the independent scoring path (A), and the pre-registered evaluation design including the derangement control (B).

3.1 Problem formulation and the design-intent header

Let a parametric CAD program PP be a sequence of sketch-extrude operations. Following the DeepCAD corpus convention Wu et al. (2021), each JSON construction history is transpiled by a deterministic script into a CadQuery-style sketch-extrude program — a Python code string of moveTo/lineTo/circle/extrude calls — and the model consumes the header-plus-program string through the base code LLM’s own subword tokenizer; 𝐱\mathbf{x} denotes that encoding. (The transpiled language covers the core sketch-extrude subset — straight-line and full-circle profiles with extrusions; arcs are approximated by straight segments and each sketch keeps its outer profile — and the five features below are defined over this language.) Design intent is formalized as a sparse binary vector ℐ∈{0,1}5\mathcal{I}\in\{0,1\}^{5} over five geometric properties — CIRCLE (a circular profile), NGON (a polygonal loop), THIN / TALL (aspect-ratio thresholds), MULTI_PART (intended multi-solid geometry) — extracted by a deterministic regex-based function ϕ:P↦ℐ\phi:P\mapsto\mathcal{I} over the program text, requiring no human annotation. Concretely, ϕ\phi pattern-matches the program text: CIRCLE is triggered by a full-circle profile call, NGON by a closed profile loop with ≥\geq5 straight segments, THIN/TALL by the ratio of extrude depth to the largest planar extent of the profile (<0.3 / >2.0 respectively), and MULTI_PART by more than one extrude block — an intent proxy that cannot itself see whether the extrudes fuse into one solid, the under-determination §3.5 addresses. CADCON prepends a header h⁡(ℐ)h(\mathcal{I}) to the program and fine-tunes with the standard causal cross-entropy loss over the concatenation z=(h⁡(ℐ),𝐱)z=(h(\mathcal{I}),\mathbf{x}), header tokens included; the model thus learns pθ(𝐱∣h(ℐ),𝐱:k)p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}\mid h(\mathcal{I}),\mathbf{x}_{:k}), where the program prefix — the first 40% of the program text, a character-level strict prefix (empty in the 0% regime) — is supplied only at evaluation: training always sees complete header-plus-program sequences. The same extractor ϕ\phi defines both the training-time headers and the original regex adherence metric — the circularity that §3.5 breaks on the produced side.

3.2 Data and representation

The corpus derives from DeepCAD (~180,000 models as JSON sketch-extrude histories; in DeepCAD’s native 256-token serialization these have mean length ≈\approx150 and maximum 1,024 tokens). Before splitting, exact- and loose-hash deduplication filters the held-out side against train: of 15,848 candidate held-out programs, 6,406 were identified as train-leaked and removed, leaving 9,442 clean held-out programs. Training uses 10,000 programs from the (unmodified) training partition; evaluation uses a frozen 100-program held-out set drawn from the 9,442 clean programs (86 with at least one active intent feature; 76 with non-empty four-feature intent, §3.6). Each history is transpiled to a CadQuery-style program (§3.1); under the base model’s tokenizer every training sequence fits complete — EOS included — within the 1,024-token cap of Table 1. Two header tokenizations test whether conditioning behavior depends on surface form: token — the active features as dedicated special tokens wrapped in delimiters (<CONSTRAINTS> <CIRCLE> <THIN> </CONSTRAINTS>; at most 7 added special tokens, whose embeddings are warm-started from the mean pretrained embeddings of their natural-language names) — and text — a single comment line naming the active features in plain words (# design intent: circle thin). Both are prepended to the front of the program text.

3.3 Model M, the unconditioned baseline, and the CFG variant

Model M is the system under diagnosis: a conditioned generator built in the pattern of current LLM-fine-tuning practice (CADmium, FlexCAD, CAD-HLLM; §2.1–2.2) — a pretrained code LLM fine-tuned on programs with a conditioning signal prepended, here produced automatically by ϕ\phi. Three design choices define it. First, M is trained exclusively on consistent pairs (h⁡(ℐi),Pi)(h(\mathcal{I}_{i}),P_{i}): every header is derived from its own program and is thus consistent with it under ϕ\phi, so the training signal rewards learning the header↔\leftrightarrowprogram correlation — M is given both the opportunity and the incentive to acquire the header→\rightarrowprogram mapping whose causal role §4.4 tests. Second, the header participates in the loss (§3.1), so M models the header jointly with the program rather than treating it as fixed context. Third, M is instantiated under both header tokenizations (token and text, §3.2), so that conclusions about conditioning do not hinge on a particular surface form. The hypothesis M carries into evaluation is directly testable: if conditioning is content-sensitive, M’s outputs should track header content — separating correct from wrong headers — and not merely header presence.

Concretely, M fine-tunes Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B Hui et al. (2024), a decoder-only Transformer code LLM, with QLoRA-style adapters Dettmers et al. (2023) — the base model quantized to 4-bit (NF4, double quantization, bfloat16 compute), with LoRA on all attention and MLP projections (rank 16, α=32\alpha=32, dropout 0.05; ≈\approx18.5M adapter parameters, ~1.2% of the base model — the resized token embedding and LM head are additionally saved so the newly added header-token rows can train, with all pre-existing embedding rows gradient-frozen), batch size 4 with gradient accumulation 8 (effective 32), learning rate 2×10−42\times 10^{-4} with linear decay over 3 epochs, gradient clipping at norm 1.0, 3 seeds per condition. The unconditioned baseline is trained identically but with no header — the never-header-trained reference for every wrong-vs-none contrast. A CADCON-CFG variant applies classifier-free-guidance-style header dropout during training (with probability 0.5 the header is replaced by a null-content placeholder) — adapting classifier-free guidance from its diffusion-training origin Ho and Salimans (2022), rather than the inference-time-only formulation of Sanchez et al. (2023), to autoregressive CAD fine-tuning — designed to permit unconditional fallback at inference; its geometric re-evaluation is left to future work (§5). Table 1 lists the full configuration; it covers M, the baseline, and the derangement control R (§3.7), which differs from M only in the header↔\leftrightarrowprogram pairing of its training data.

3.4 GRPO validity-reward study

To probe whether reinforcement learning moves geometric validity independently of adherence, Group Relative Policy Optimization is applied on top of the SFT model with a binary validity reward (1 iff the program executes in CadQuery within 10 s and yields a non-empty solid; G=4G=4 completions per prompt, learning rate 5×10−75\times 10^{-7}, 100 steps, entropy coefficient 0.01). Lightweight proxy-reward variants were also trained to reduce oracle executions; the supporting observation of §4.5 uses the oracle-reward run and does not depend on the proxy details.

3.5 Independent geometry-side adherence metric

Our initial adherence metric applied the same regex feature extractor ϕ\phi used to build the headers, both to the ground-truth intent and to the generated program text; a single-condition audit bounded but did not remove the resulting circularity. Here we adopt a metric that shares no code with ϕ\phi. Each generated program is executed in an isolated CadQuery subprocess (10 s timeout); on the produced B-rep solid, five executable assertions read the realized features — CIRCLE from a circular edge, NGON from a face with ≥\geq5 straight edges, THIN/TALL from the executed bounding-box aspect ratio, MULTI_PART from the solid count — grouped per requirement in the style of CADTests Mallis et al. (2026). A program that fails to execute realizes no features (execution-inclusive scoring). The intent target remains ϕ\phi(GT), which defines the task; only the produced-side scoring changes, breaking the produced-side circularity that the earlier audit could only bound. MULTI_PART is reported but excluded from the primary metric: on execution it is geometrically under-determined — overlapping extrudes fuse to one solid; in the pre-registration audit, 6/26 executable ground-truth MULTI_PART programs realize >1 solid and 0/62 generated, and in the frozen evaluation run itself 0 of 1,068 executable generated samples with a MULTI_PART intent realize >1 solid — so the primary metric is a four-feature macro-recall. The metric is not gameable by feature-spamming: in no arm do executable outputs realize more than ~1.1 distinct primary features on average (unconditioned baseline 1.11; header-informed arms 0.72–0.96; masked arms 0.00–0.41; conditional on realizing at least one feature, 1.0–1.3 in every arm), so recall is not inflated by emitting everything. The primary decision uses this metric; the regex metric is retained only as an explicit circularity comparison.

3.6 Pre-registered six-cell evaluation

We evaluate a {0%, 40%} program-prefix ×\times {correct, wrong, masked} header matrix, for both tokenizations, over three seeds, plus the never-header-trained unconditioned baseline at both prefixes — (6 header cells ×\times 2 tokenizations + 2 baseline cells) ×\times 3 seeds = 42 pure-inference jobs on the frozen 100-program held-out set; generation is batched greedy decoding (no sampling), up to 768 new tokens (Table 1); four-feature recall on the 76 programs with non-empty four-feature intent. The 40% character-level prefix sits below the earliest feature signature in the programs (median first occurrence of the five signatures lies at 52–87% of program length), consistent with the low prefix feature-leakage measured in our initial evaluation (<10%; §6). The wrong header is a well-formed header taken from another sample (correct content replaced by incorrect content, seed-fixed). The masked header (absent at inference) suppresses the header for a model trained with one. Decision rules — same-seed paired Wilcoxon (pratt, one-sided, asymptotic) at p<0.05, ≥\geq2/3-seed direction and significance for the text side, ≥\geq2/3-seed direction for the token side, a reverse-direction veto, and a profile-level direction guardrail (intent profiles: the six intent-feature combinations observed in the held-out set; Appendix C) — were frozen with sha256 before any scoring; the pre-registration document is part of the release (§ Reproducibility).

3.7 Causal control: the derangement-trained model R

A wrong-header harm (§4.2) is causally ambiguous: it could show that the model reads the header’s content, or merely that a mismatched header is an out-of-distribution input for a header-trained model. The control that separates these must experience wrong headers as in-distribution while having had no consistent header↔\leftrightarrowprogram relationship to learn from. We construct it by derangement training. Model R is M’s causal twin, designed to satisfy three properties at once: (i) identical training recipe — the same base model, LoRA configuration, training programs, step count, and seeds as M (Table 1), so a behavioral difference between the two cannot be attributed to the training recipe — architecturally, R is indistinguishable from M; (ii) identical header marginal — every training program receives another program’s header under a fixed derangement plan, so every header string R sees is byte-identical in form and frequency to what M sees, and a wrong header at evaluation is not a rare or novel input for R; (iii) no learnable mapping — the derangement destroys the header↔\leftrightarrowprogram correlation, so R cannot systematically acquire the mapping whose causal role is under test. The destruction is not perfect: the small feature vocabulary leaves 8.8–9.7% of deranged training headers correct-by-chance (measured per seed on the 10,000 training programs: 8.8% / 9.7% / 9.2%), a residual that biases R toward content-sensitivity — making any observed immunity of R conservative. If the harm in §4.2 is a marginal/mechanical perturbation effect, R — a model for which uncorrelated headers are the training distribution itself — should be hurt by wrong headers too; if the harm requires the learned header→\rightarrowprogram mapping, R should be immune — predictions that are evidential only if R remains competent, which the pre-registered gate below verifies.

The analysis was pre-registered and frozen before R’s evaluation data existed: the protocol and analysis script (f4_analysis.py, sha256 c506ab4e…) were frozen on 2026-07-07, R’s evaluations ran on 2026-07-08, and no threshold or rule was altered after freezing. The protocol pre-registers, in order: (i) a competence gate — R must stay non-trivially above the 40%-prefix floor (per-seed adherence ≥\geq 0.30 in both header arms, a floor chosen ex-ante with the baseline ≈\approx 0.425 known, deliberately below it because a correlation-deprived control is expected to be weaker than an unconditioned model; and executability within 0.10 of baseline) — which guards against a spurious dissociation from a broken control; (ii) the dissociation test (Test D) — the per-sample interaction between M’s and R’s correct→\rightarrowwrong adherence drop, paired Wilcoxon per seed, requiring ≥\geq2/3 seeds positive and significant with a reverse-direction veto; and (iii) two guardrails — an executable-intersection re-analysis that removes the execution-inclusive zero-filling entirely, and a profile-level direction check. The protocol additionally pre-registers a supporting-only, content-graded dose-response probe on M — a corrupted arm (one or two primary features falsified) and a random arm (well-formed, size-matched, sample-unrelated feature sets; designated non-evidential ex ante) — whose criterion and descriptive outcome are reported in §4.4. A built-in assertion re-reads the frozen §4.1–4.3 scores and checks that M’s arm means match the published values — a wiring/anti-drift integrity check (it re-reads the same frozen artifacts, so it is not an independent reproduction).

4 Results

We report the geometry-side metric (§3.5) as primary; regex-side numbers appear beside it to expose circularity. All adherence numbers are four-feature macro-recall over the 76 non-empty-intent programs, mean over three seeds. Per-feature positive counts in this set are CIRCLE 24, NGON 30, THIN 44, TALL 4; TALL is sparse, so its per-feature estimates are noisy and no per-feature TALL claim is made. At the profile level, the pure-CIRCLE and TALL profiles are floored at baseline for the wrong-vs-none contrast (adherence 0.00 in both the baseline and wrong-header arms; TALL reaches 1.00 only under a correct header), so headline statements about the harm refer to the polygonal and thin profiles (full per-profile analysis: Appendix C). Models: M (standard, informative-header-trained), R (derangement control, §3.7). Header arms at evaluation: correct, wrong (= another program’s GT header, shuffled in at evaluation), corrupted / random (dose-response probes, §4.4), masked (absent at inference), and the unconditioned baseline (never header-trained).

4.1 Intent conditioning genuinely uses the header but is partly over-credited by the regex metric

Two observations (Figure 2; full numbers in Table 2). First, conditioning genuinely uses the header: at 0% prefix the unconditioned baseline cannot generate valid CAD at all (0.000), while a correct header drives adherence to 0.50 (token) / 0.78 (text) — the header alone carries the generation. Second, the independent metric deflates the apparent conditioning benefit: at 40% prefix the correct-header gain over baseline shrinks from +0.235 (regex) to +0.132 (geom) for text, and from +0.207 to +0.018 for token — i.e. much of the token-header “benefit” the regex reports does not survive as realized geometry. This confirms, rather than merely bounds, a partial metric circularity in conditioning claims scored by their own feature detector.

4.2 A wrong header hurts more than no header (independent metric, conditional-completion regime)

At 40% prefix the ordering under the independent metric is correct > none > wrong (the correct>none leg established on the text side only, §4.1): a wrong header degrades geometric adherence below the no-header baseline (0.425 →\rightarrow 0.305 text, 0.215 token). The drop is direction-unanimous across all three seeds and both tokenizations; the token side is strongly significant on every seed (paired Wilcoxon p = 6.8×10−66.8\times 10^{-6} / 1.8×10−51.8\times 10^{-5} / 8.0×10−48.0\times 10^{-4} across seeds 0/1/2), the text side is significant on 2/3 seeds (p = 0.073 / 0.014 / 0.003 across seeds 0/1/2; the non-significant seed 0 is direction-consistent), with no reverse-direction violation and a passing profile-level guardrail (mean profile effect −-0.078). As in the headline claim, the effect is established on design intents the model can render unconditioned (polygonal / thin); the pure-CIRCLE and TALL profiles are floored at baseline and uninformative for this contrast (§4 preamble; Appendix C). The masked arm also falls below baseline (0.263 text / 0.237 token) — the signature of learned, harmful header-dependence, now confirmed under the independent metric.

The effect is not a validity artifact. On the subset where both the baseline and the wrong-header arm produce valid, executable geometry, the wrong-header adherence deficit persists on every seed and both tokenizations (mean difference −-0.155 / −-0.230 / −-0.273 text, significant on 2/3 seeds (p = 0.061 / 0.005 / 2×10−42\times 10^{-4}); −-0.288 / −-0.250 / −-0.284 token). Given the same prefix and equally valid output geometry, a wrong header still steers the model away from the design intent.

Non-tied pairs. Under greedy decoding most held-out programs are byte-identical across arms and therefore tie; we report the non-tied pairs (harmful / helpful / tied over the 76 programs) so the effect is not overstated. For wrong-header vs. baseline the harmful direction dominates the non-tied pairs: token 19/0/57, 20/1/55, 19/4/53 across seeds (nearly every non-tied pair is harmful, hence p ≤\leq 8×10−48\times 10^{-4} on every seed); text 12/6/58, 16/6/54, 16/4/56 (harmful-dominant but noisier). The effect thus rests on ~15–25 non-tied pairs per seed; the remaining ~50–60 programs generate identical geometry with or without the wrong header. The positive control (correct vs. baseline) is correspondingly noisy for the token header (16/8, 12/18, 16/16), consistent with the deflated token-header benefit of §4.1.

That a wrong header hurts does not yet say why — §4.4 shows the harm requires the learned header→\rightarrowprogram mapping.

4.3 The harm is specific to the conditional-completion regime

At 0% prefix the picture inverts: the unconditioned baseline is floored (0/100 executable, adherence 0.000), so a wrong header — which still yields some executable, partially-adhering programs (0.160 text / 0.077 token) — scores above baseline. “Wrong < none” is undefined when “none” cannot generate at all. The wrong-header harm is therefore a property of the conditional-completion regime, where a meaningful unconditioned reference exists; we state this scope explicitly rather than claim a universal effect.

4.4 The harm requires the learned header→program mapping: a derangement-control dissociation

The wrong<baseline result of §4.2 admits two readings — semantic misdirection by the header’s content, or a mere distribution-shift/mismatch perturbation that would derail any header-trained model. The derangement control R of §3.7 separates them: if the harm is mechanical, R should be hurt too; if it requires the learned mapping, R should be immune. All analyses below follow the frozen protocol of §3.7; except where noted (the 0%-prefix within-M probe, drawn from the §4.1–4.3 evaluation), all are text-side headers, 40% prefix, 3 seeds.

R is competent, and its competence does not hinge on the gate thresholds. R passes the pre-registered competence gate on every seed (correct-header adherence 0.355 / 0.408 / 0.355 and wrong-header 0.362 / 0.414 / 0.414, all ≥\geq the ex-ante floor of 0.30; executability 0.535 (pooled over R’s correct- and wrong-header arms) vs. baseline 0.553, within the pre-set 0.10 margin — R sits ≈\approx1.8 points below baseline). Floor-independent evidence says the same thing: on its executable outputs R’s adherence is 0.71, statistically indistinguishable from the baseline’s executable-only 0.77 (Mann–Whitney two-sided p = 0.24, n = 120 vs 126) yet strictly below M’s 0.94 (two-sided p = 1.6×10−81.6\times 10^{-8}) — exactly the profile of a competent but correlation-deprived control, not a floored one.

Test D: M is hurt, R is not. M’s correct→\rightarrowwrong drop is 0.184 / 0.289 / 0.283 per seed; R’s is −-0.007 / −-0.007 / −-0.059 (≈\approx0) (Figure 3; Table 3). The per-sample interaction (drop_M −- drop_R) is positive and significant on 3/3 seeds (paired Wilcoxon p = 4.2×10−34.2\times 10^{-3} / 6.7×10−66.7\times 10^{-6} / 3.6×10−63.6\times 10^{-6}; mean interaction 0.191 / 0.296 / 0.342), with no reverse-direction veto and no underpowered seed (26 / 26 / 32 non-zero pairs of 76). Seed 0 is the weakest — significant but marginal (p = 4.2×10−34.2\times 10^{-3}; it survives even the two most adversarial sign-flips at p = 0.034 and loses significance only at three; a plain sign test loses significance at two) — while seeds 1–2 are overwhelming (p < 10−510^{-5}) and satisfy the pre-registered ≥\geq2/3 rule by themselves: dropping seed 0 entirely, Test D still passes. Both pre-registered guardrails hold: on the executable intersection (all four arms executable; N = 87 sample×\timesseed pairs pooled over the three seeds: 20/33/34), where the execution-inclusive zero-filling is removed entirely, the interaction grows (mean 0.391) — the zero-fill is the conservative direction, not the source of the effect; and the profile-level effect is ≥\geq0 (0.310 unweighted over six profiles; 0.276 sample-weighted). Full robustness of Test D — five zero-handling treatments, a diff-mass decomposition, and leave-one-profile-out — is reported in Appendix B.

The most direct view: R emits the same geometry either way. On jointly-executable outputs, R realizes an identical geometric feature set under correct and wrong headers on 93% / 71% / 98% of samples per seed (28/30, 30/42, 41/42; Figure 4); M does so on only 35–43% (13/33, 15/43, 18/42). In this completion regime the control does not route header content into generation; the standard model does.

Within-M affirmative evidence that the header content is read. At 0% prefix, M with a correct header reconstructs the intent at 0.776 adherence (Table 4a); with the header masked, the same model on seeds 1–2 still executes (96–100% of outputs run) yet realizes zero intent (0.000) — runnable programs, no reconstructed design intent — while on seed 0 masking collapses execution entirely (0/100, matching the unconditioned baseline). In no seed does the masked model realize any intent: content, not merely field presence, carries the information. This evidence is internal to M and independent of the control.

What a mechanical-perturbation account would predict — and what we observe. If a wrong header simply derailed generation, we would expect degraded executability and regression toward the unconditioned baseline (information loss). Instead (Table 4b): wrong-header executability (0.645) is higher than the no-header baseline’s (0.553) — wrong headers yield more runnable programs whose geometry adheres less to the true intent; on the executable intersection the wrong-header arm sits below baseline (§4.2: −-0.155 / −-0.230 / −-0.273, significant on 2/3 seeds) — active misdirection, not information loss; and the harm is not a step function of mismatch: the content-graded comparison — correct vs. corrupted (one or two primary features falsified) — holds on 2/3 seeds (p = 0.091 / 3×10−43\times 10^{-4} / 1×10−31\times 10^{-3}), while wrong headers (real but mismatched) hurt less than random ones (valid feature sets in unnatural, sample-unrelated combinations) on 3/3 seeds (p = 0.011 / 0.006 / 0.040) — a contrast that grades header naturalness rather than content, reported descriptively. We note for completeness that the pre-registered dose-response criterion — requiring both correct>corrupted and corrupted>wrong at ≥\geq2/3 seeds — was not confirmed (corrupted>wrong reached significance on 1/3 seeds; the random arm hurt more than the wrong arm on all seeds); the graded observations above are descriptive support, not a rescued dose-response claim.

Conclusion of the control. A competent model that could not have learned the header→\rightarrowprogram mapping is immune to wrong headers; the model that learned the mapping is hurt by them. The harm therefore requires the learned mapping: the marginal/mechanical distribution-shift confound is excluded. (What remains within scope and what does not — in particular the joint-consistency reading — is discussed in §5.) The report-only content-blindness probe (R correct-vs-wrong, per-seed −-0.007 / −-0.007 / −-0.059) is consistent with immunity; the seed-2 value is an execution-artifact of four zero-filled samples and vanishes on the executable intersection (−-0.012, n.s.; Appendix A).

4.5 Validity vs. adherence orthogonality

An accompanying GRPO experiment — in which a binary validity reward raised validity without moving adherence — is retained as a supporting observation; at the training scale studied (100 GRPO steps) we do not read it as a fundamental orthogonality, and we read it alongside the code-RL literature’s treatment of executability and semantic adherence as distinct reward channels.

5 Discussion

The independent metric changes the paper’s center of gravity in a way that strengthens it. The headline positive result under the self-referential regex metric — a large adherence gain from conditioning — is partly an over-credit of the regex metric, most starkly for the token header, whose realized-geometry benefit at 40% prefix is negligible. Being explicit about this is the honest cost of an independent metric. What survives, and is the more consequential finding, is the negative one, now causally grounded: in the regime where a designer would actually use such a model — completing or editing an existing partial program — supplying a semantically wrong design-intent header is worse than supplying none, and §4.4 shows this is a property of the learned header→\rightarrowprogram mapping, not of receiving an odd input. A system that trusts a possibly-wrong intent field will not merely be perturbed by it as noise; it will be semantically misled — steered, competently and executably, away from the true design intent.

What the control does and does not exclude. The derangement control equalizes the header marginal, so it excludes explanations in which a wrong header hurts merely by being a rare, malformed, or length-shifted input — the marginal/mechanical confound. It cannot exclude a subtler reading: for M (trained only on consistent header/program pairs) a wrong header creates a jointly atypical (header, prefix) input, so one may posit that M detects the inconsistency and degrades, rather than “believing” the wrong content. We do not separate graded semantic reading from learned consistency-checking here, and the pre-registered dose-response probe that might have (§4.4) did not confirm. We note only that detecting a header/prefix inconsistency itself requires representing the header’s content — so either reading places header content, not input oddity, in the causal path; and the observed signature (executability up, adherence below baseline) is that of misdirection rather than derailment.

This is the natural-language distractor phenomenon Tao and Agrawal (2026) instantiated in structured geometric program generation, and it motivates the same remedy: a conditioning interface that can fall back to unconditioned behavior when intent is absent or suspect. Our header-dropout variant is one cheap training-side step in that direction, and a decode-time backoff in the spirit of Tao and Agrawal (2026) is a natural next one; we leave their geometric evaluation to future work.

6 Limitations

  • •

    Regime and prefix coupling. The wrong<none effect holds in the 40%-prefix conditional-completion regime, not the 0%-prefix from-scratch regime; and the 40% setting couples the effect to information carried by the program prefix (feature-leakage measured at below 10% in our initial evaluation, but a coupling nonetheless). We do not claim a prefix-independent effect.

  • •

    Intent-space coverage. The effect is established on renderable intents (polygonal / thin); the pure-CIRCLE and TALL profiles sit at a baseline generation floor (baseline and wrong-header adherence both 0.00; TALL reaches 1.00 only under a correct header) and are uninformative for the contrast; MULTI_PART is excluded from the primary metric as geometrically under-determined; per-feature TALL (n=4 positives) carries no individual claim. The primary metric is a four-feature, three-valued macro-recall — a coarse instrument.

  • •

    Evaluation scale. The held-out set is 100 programs (76 with non-empty four-feature intent). Scaling the evaluation and adopting a public executable benchmark (e.g., CADTests/CADBench families) is the primary planned strengthening before a camera-ready.

  • •

    Baselines. The derangement control (training-time shuffled-header control) is done (§3.7/§4.4). A natural-language-prompt baseline remains future work.

  • •

    Scale. A single 1.5B model on DeepCAD; whether the deflation of conditioning benefit and the wrong<none harm persist at larger scale and on other program representations (native DeepCAD token sequences, richer B-rep or code formats) is open.

  • •

    Control margins. R’s competence clears pre-registered thresholds that were frozen before its data existed, but not by a wide margin (adherence floor cleared by +0.055 on the binding seed; executability ≈\approx1.8 points below baseline within a 0.10 margin); the floor-independent evidence of §4.4 is therefore reported alongside. The derangement leaves ~9% of training headers correct-by-chance (8.8–9.7% measured per seed), a residual that biases the control toward content-sensitivity and makes its observed immunity conservative.

  • •

    Integrity note. The regex-side numbers of correct/masked/baseline cells at 40% prefix differ from the original run by 2–6 samples per cell (their reference values came from a different historical eval code path); the 0%-prefix cells and the decision-critical wrong-header cells reproduce exactly, and the geometry-side decision is computed entirely within this internally-consistent run. The control pipeline’s built-in check (§3.7) that M’s arm means match the §4.1–4.3 values is a wiring/anti-drift integrity check, not an independent reproduction.

7 Reproducibility and release

Both evaluation protocols were pre-registered: decision rules, statistical tests, thresholds, and analysis scripts were frozen (with SHA-256 hashes recorded) before the corresponding evaluation data existed — the six-cell protocol before any scoring, and the control protocol (f4_analysis.py) the day before the control model’s evaluations ran — and no rule was changed afterwards. We release the frozen analysis scripts with their hash manifest, the frozen held-out list (including the 76-program analysis subset and the six profile definitions), the complete raw per-sample geometry scores (geom_scores.jsonl for all arms and seeds) from which every number in this paper can be recomputed, and the figure/table scripts that recompute them. All experiments ran on a single consumer workstation with two RTX 3090 GPUs (24 GB each): the two pre-registered evaluation suites are pure inference (42 and 18 jobs; ≈\approx6 and ≈\approx2 wall-clock hours on both GPUs respectively), and each LoRA fine-tuning run (M, baseline, and R variants; 3 seeds each) completes in single-digit GPU-hours. LoRA adapter checkpoints for all reported conditions will be released upon acceptance.

8 Conclusion

This paper built a controlled diagnostic around a deliberately representative conditioned generator: CADCON, a five-feature design-intent header prepended to CadQuery-style sketch-extrude programs and fine-tuned into a 1.5B code LLM on consumer hardware (model M, §3.3). Two instruments carry the diagnosis. The first is an execution-level adherence metric that scores the produced B-rep solid and shares no code with the extractor that defines the headers (§3.5), removing the produced-side circularity of self-referential evaluation. The second is a derangement-trained causal twin, R — identical training recipe, identical header marginal, no consistent header↔\leftrightarrowprogram relationship to learn (§3.7) — which turns “does the model read the header?” into a testable contrast. Every decision rule was pre-registered and frozen before scoring: the {0%, 40%}-prefix ×\times {correct, wrong, masked} matrix over both tokenizations and three seeds, and the control’s competence gate and dissociation test.

Four results emerge, each computed under a frozen, pre-registered protocol. (i) Under the independent metric, a semantically wrong header degrades adherence below the no-header baseline in conditional completion (0.425 →\rightarrow 0.305 text / 0.215 token), direction-unanimous across three seeds and both tokenizations, on the intents the model can render unconditioned. (ii) The harm is causal in the precise sense the control can test (text headers): M’s correct→\rightarrowwrong drop (0.18–0.29 per seed) dissociates from R’s (≈\approx0) on 3/3 seeds (p ≤\leq 4.2×10−34.2\times 10^{-3}) — the damage requires the learned header→\rightarrowprogram mapping, and the marginal/mechanical distribution-shift confound is excluded. (iii) The apparent benefit of a correct header is partly metric circularity: the token-header gain collapses from +0.21 under the training-side regex to +0.02 under realized geometry. (iv) The effect is a property of the conditional-completion regime — at 0% prefix the unconditioned baseline cannot generate valid CAD at all, and the contrast is undefined.

The two evaluation habits this diagnosis interrogates — scoring conditioning with a signal-derived metric, and evaluating only correct signals — each concealed something: the first inflated the benefit, the second hid an active hazard. Correcting both re-centers the headline: the durable result is not the benefit of a correct header — real on the text side, negligible for the token header — but that a model which has learned to rely on an intent field is actively misdirected by that field when it is wrong — producing competent, executable geometry that adheres to the true intent less than if the field were absent — on the intents it can render unconditioned, on the workflow such models are built to support. To our knowledge this is the first causally-controlled isolation of wrong-content-worse-than-no-content in structured geometric program generation, and it locates the failure where repair can act: in the learned conditioning interface, not in input hygiene.

For LLM-based parametric CAD generation specifically, three consequences follow. For builders: a conditioning field — a text description, a structured header, an upstream model’s inferred plan — must be treated as untrusted input, with the fallback to unconditioned behavior built into the training interface, not into post-hoc filtering. For evaluators: a conditioning claim should answer three questions before it is believed — does the benefit survive a conditioning-independent, execution-level metric; is a wrong signal worse than none; and is the harm mapping-dependent? This audit pair answers all three on a consumer workstation: the evaluations are pure inference, and the derangement control adds one fine-tuning run per seed at single-digit GPU-hours. For the field’s trajectory: whether the deflated benefit and the wrong-header harm survive larger models, other program representations, and richer intent languages is now a sharp, testable question. Intent conditioning for CAD is worth building; interfaces that degrade gracefully to unconditioned behavior when intent is absent or wrong are worth building first.

Appendix

Appendix A Pre-registration record and report-only probes

Freeze chain. The six-cell protocol (decision rules, tests, thresholds) was frozen with SHA-256 hashes before any scoring; the control protocol and its analysis script (f4_analysis.py, sha256 c506ab4e…) were frozen on 2026-07-07, before the control model’s evaluations ran on 2026-07-08. No rule, threshold, or test was altered after freezing. The released hash manifest covers the analysis scripts, the frozen held-out list (100 programs; the 76-program four-feature analysis subset; the six profile definitions), and both evaluation-job lists (42 six-cell jobs; 18 control jobs).

Report-only content-blindness probe (M1) and the seed-2 artifact. R’s correct-vs-wrong adherence difference (execution-inclusive) is −-0.007 / −-0.007 / −-0.059 per seed; the note attached to this probe in the frozen protocol expects ≈\approx0. The seed-2 value −-0.059 (nominal p = 0.013) is an execution artifact of exactly four zero-filled samples (held-out indices 56, 76, 77, 97: R-correct failed to execute and was scored 0 while R-wrong executed): on the executable intersection the difference collapses to −-0.012 (1 non-zero pair, n.s.), and the per-seed signs on the intersection are inconsistent (0.000 / +0.060 / −-0.012). M1 feeds neither the competence gate nor Test D; the ruling is unchanged by it. The presence probe (R correct-vs-masked: 0.000 / +0.066 / −-0.053) is a presence control and, per the frozen protocol, is not citable as content evidence.

Appendix B Robustness of Test D

Zero-handling robustness. The per-seed Test D interaction under five treatments of the tie-heavy diff distribution. Test D remains significant on every seed under all five; the frozen choice (pratt) retains the tie-heavy zero mass rather than discarding it, though it is not uniformly the largest p in each row (e.g. the seed-0 sign test gives 1.4×10−21.4\times 10^{-2}).

Diff-mass decomposition. The zero mass is genuine no-effect samples, not hidden cancellation; the non-zero pairs are dominated by the causal-control cell (M perturbed, R immune).

(Pairs where both models move without exactly cancelling — 0/3/3 per seed — are classified only by their interaction sign, so the sign columns, not the first four, total the 26/26/32 non-zero pairs.)

Leave-one-profile-out. Test D re-run with each profile’s samples removed. The dissociation survives every removal under the pre-registered ≥\geq2/3 rule — including all NGON samples (the largest profile; with NGON removed, seed 0 stays direction-positive but loses significance at p = 0.32 while seeds 1–2 remain at p ≤\leq 1.3×10−31.3\times 10^{-3}) and all circle-containing samples (3/3 significant).

Further checks. (i) Profile-weighting: the profile-level guardrail passes both unweighted (0.310) and sample-size-weighted (0.276); Test D itself is a per-sample pooled test independent of profile weighting. (ii) Executable-only view: removing the execution-inclusive zero-fill enlarges the interaction — with each arm averaged over its own executable outputs, (dropM −- dropR) is +0.47/+0.51/+0.49 per seed, and on the four-arm executable intersection it is 0.391 (N = 87); R’s executable-only adherence is 0.708 (n = 120) vs. the baseline’s 0.770 (n = 126; Mann–Whitney two-sided p = 0.24) and M’s 0.941 (n = 135; p = 1.6×10−81.6\times 10^{-8}). (iii) Header length: the correlation between M’s per-sample drop and the header-length change (characters) is r ≈\approx 0.26 (≈\approx7% of variance), and the identical derangement plan is applied to both M’s and R’s evaluations, so length is matched across the interaction’s two arms. (iv) The metric is not gameable by feature-spamming (§3.5).

Appendix C Per-profile detail and dose-response

Per-profile means (text headers, 40% prefix; seed-averaged). The wrong-vs-none contrast is floored at the pure-CIRCLE and TALL profiles (baseline = wrong = 0.00); the dissociation (last column) is carried by the polygonal/thin profiles, with TALL contributing only via its correct arm.

Dose-response (supporting; pre-registered criterion not confirmed). Arm means: correct 0.557 > corrupted 0.393 > wrong 0.305 > random 0.219. Per-seed one-sided p: correct>corrupted 0.091 / 3×10−43\times 10^{-4} / 1×10−31\times 10^{-3} (2/3); corrupted>wrong 0.074 / 0.056 / 0.038 (1/3 — the pre-registered monotone criterion therefore fails); wrong>random 0.011 / 0.006 / 0.040 (3/3; grades naturalness, not content; the random arm was designated non-evidential ex ante).

Non-tied pairs (wrong vs. baseline; harmful/helpful/tied of 76). Token: 19/0/57, 20/1/55, 19/4/53. Text: 12/6/58, 16/6/54, 16/4/56. Positive control (correct vs. baseline, token): 16/8, 12/18, 16/16.
